title: What it doesn't show
hookLine: many early studies were small, and the effects are often modest

lines: A GLOWING BRAIN ON A COVER.
REBUILDS YOUR BRAIN IN EIGHT WEEKS.
cards: A glowing brain on a magazine cover, lit up in orange and blue, beside a person sitting cross-legged in front of a sunrise. The headline: meditation rebuilds your brain in eight weeks.

Covers like that aren't hard to find. It's a beautiful picture. And it's one reason a group of scientists who study meditation, people who believe it's worth studying, wrote a paper warning everyone to calm down.
Yesterday was what the research shows. Today is the other half, just as important.

teach.b: In 2018 fifteen researchers, led by Nicholas Van Dam, published a paper called Mind the Hype, in the journal Perspectives on Psychological Science. Several of them study meditation themselves.
In plain terms, here's what they said.
First, nobody agrees what mindfulness means. It can be a trait, a state, a practice, a program or a whole tradition, so two studies of mindfulness may not measure the same thing.
Second, many studies, especially the early ones, were small. Remember the coins: a study of twenty or thirty people can find a big effect just by chance.
Third, many had weak comparisons, a waitlist that did nothing instead of an active group.

teach.h: BRAIN SCANS ARE EASY TO OVER-READ.
teach.b: Fourth, brain scan studies are especially tempting to over-read. A region looks different in a small group of meditators; that doesn't mean you'll grow a new brain by Friday.
There's also a quieter problem across science: studies that find nothing are less likely to get published, so the shelf of published papers can look rosier than reality.
And the effects that do hold up are often modest, usually no bigger than other good options, like exercise or therapy. None of this says meditation is useless; yesterday's review stands.
The honest claims are just smaller than the magazine covers. That matters for a person, not only for scientists.
Expect magic, and you'll either quit when it doesn't come or blame yourself. Expect something modest and real, and you can keep going. No magic.

how: Researchers now call for larger trials, active control groups, clear definitions of mindfulness and cautious reporting, and some teachers present meditation's benefits as modest.

o: a teacher who said meditation can rebuild the brain in weeks
a monk who wrote that mindfulness has one fixed meaning
a researcher who warned that meditation's benefits get overhyped

games.q: mind the hype — tap the pairs.

s: Mind the Hype was written by critics who reject meditation
its authors include researchers who study meditation and think it's worth studying.
brain scans of small groups prove meditation rebuilds the brain
small scan studies are easy to over-read.
studies finding nothing are less likely to be published
so the published record can look rosier than reality.

games.q: you started meditating expecting to be transformed in a month. it hasn't happened. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: expect something modest and real, and keep going.
games.why: honest expectations keep you practicing: the effects that hold up are real but usually modest.

practice: Notice any hope you've been carrying about practice, that it will fix your sleep, or your temper, or make you a calmer person by spring, and name it kindly.
Then set it down beside you, like a bag you don't need to carry into the room. Sit without it: just breath, just attention, asking nothing of these minutes.

wordCard.voice: Van Dam, lead author of the Mind the Hype warning that many early meditation studies were small, comparisons weak, and effects modest.

carryVoice: Your line: no magic. A big claim always earns one question: how big was the study? That's day three hundred six.
